newsitem.title: MALTA: Anti-EU Labour claims victory in Malta.
newsitem.headline: Anti-EU Labour claims victory in Malta.

text.p: Malta's Labour Party claimed victory in general elections after a campaign in which it pledged to abandon the country's application to join to European Union and to scrap a highly-unpopular value added tax.

"There are clear indications that there is a Labour victory and I want to reaffirm our intention to form a government for all the people of Malta and Gozo," party leader Alfred Sant, 48, said on radio late on Sunday.
The Nationalist Party of Prime Minister Edward Fenech Adami, which had a three-seat majority in the outgoing 65-member parliament, had no immediate comment.
Feneech Adami had pledged to pursue his 1990 application to join the EU and had forecast that Malta would be ready to be admitted in mid-1988.

Under the complex voting system, official results would not be known for hours. But party delegates monitoring the selection of first-preferance ballots can normally accurately predict which party, though not which candidates, has won.
Fenech Adami, 62, grim-faced, earlier told reporters at a counting centre: "The situation is still unclear.
"Predictions are subject of course to a margin of error which indeed could go either in favour of one party or the other. It is going very definitely to be a very close finish."
Labour also promised to pull the Mediterranean island state out of NATO's Partnership for Peace programme which it joined last year.
This would be followed by legislation to abolish VAT and replace it with customs tariffs, undercutting a basis of EU membership and signalling Malta's withdrawal of its bid.

Discontent with VAT, with a standard rate of 15 percent, has been widespread, both for its impact on inflation and for the perceived meddling by officialdom in traditionally secretive, family-run businesses.

Sant had worked hard to change the Labour Party's image, focusing on the hardships of ordinary people and campaigning for "positive neutrality" and a "special relationship" with Europe, instead of EU membership.
Sant called on his supporters to "observe tomorrow as a normal day" -- a pious hope judging by the mass celebrations that started earlier well before his claim of victory.

In Hamrun, near Labour Party headquarters and within shouting distance of Nationalist Party headquarters, exuberant Labour supporters blocked streets with streams of hooting vehicles laden with chanting, flag-waving supporters.
Car radios blared in a triumphant cacophony, while some supporters sang and beat on vehicle roofs.
The turnout at Saturday's poll was a record 97.163 percent of the electorate of nearly 275,000 people.
The election saw a further 15,000 young people added to the voting lists, and Sant said: "It was the youth who brought the Labour Party out on top."
